title: PARLIAMENT QUESTION: NUCLEAR POWER PROJECTS
body_text:
The details of projects under construction are tabulated below. Sr. Project Location Capacity (MW) Commissioning Date Cost (Rs. Crore) Original Status/ Revised Sanctioned Revised Indigenous Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (IPHWR) 1 RAPP-7* Rawatbhata, Rajasthan 700 Jun-2016 Commenced commercial operation on 15.04.2026 12,320 22,924 RAPP-8 700 Dec-2016 In advanced stage of commissioning (expected to be operational            in 2026) 2 GHAVP-1 Gorakhpur, Haryana 700 Sep-2020 Completion    of construction and commissioning is expected to be completed in about 6 years from First Pour of Concrete. 20,594 Under revision GHAVP-2 700 Mar-2021
3 KAIGA-5 Kaiga, Karnataka 700 June-2026 June-2031 21,000 Under revision KAIGA-6 700 June-2027 June-2032 4 PFBR Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu 500 Sep-2010 Mar- 2027 3492 Under revision Light Water Reactors (LWR) with Foreign Cooperation 5 KKNPP-3 Kudankulam, Tamil Nadu 1000 Mar-2023 Jun-2027 39,849 68,893 KKNPP-4 1000 Nov-2023 Jun-2028 6 KKNPP-5 1000 Dec-2026 Jun-2029 49,621 69,437 KKNPP-6 1000 Sep-2027 Mar-2030 *Already commenced production in April 2026. However, cost available on Twin Unit basis (RAPP-7 & RAPP-8) The year-wise details of the funds sanctioned, released and utilized for each project under construction during the last five years are attached as Annexure. The major reasons for delay in construction/ commissioning of projects in the recent past have been due to extensive design changes following the Fukushima incident in Japan, delay in supply of critical equipment, Covid-19 pandemic & related issues, delay in supplies from Russian Federation (for KKNPP), delay in execution of works by contractors at site on account of financial crunch / cash flow problems post Covid, difficult site soil conditions (at GHAVP), shortage of skilled contractor manpower, and the impact due to ongoing Russia-Ukraine and USA/ Israel-Iran geopolitical conflict. To address the challenges, various measures are being implemented to ensure timely completion of the projects. The measures include, periodic project reviews at multiple levels in NPCIL & DAE, constant monitoring of progress of project activities, timely identification of constraints & making necessary mid-course corrections, frequent meetings with vendors/ contractors to resolve various issues and re-sequencing of construction activities to the extent possible, higher delegation of powers to various executives of NPCIL and constitution of Board sub-committee for monitoring of projects. In addition to this, bulk ordering of long delivery equipment has been adopted and many equipment are under manufacturing/ progressive delivery for various reactors being implemented in fleet mode to ensure timely supply of long lead items for the projects. Upon progressive commissioning of the projects currently under construction, a cumulative capacity of 8000 MW would be added to the national grid.

enrichment.summary: In a written Rajya Sabha reply, the Department of Atomic Energy detailed the status of India's under-construction nuclear power projects, including RAPP-7&8, GHAVP-1&2, KAIGA-5&6, PFBR, and KKNPP-3,4,5&6, with revised costs and commissioning timelines. RAPP-7 commenced commercial operation on 15.04.2026, while other projects face delays attributed to post-Fukushima design changes, COVID-19, supply delays from Russia, and geopolitical conflicts. Upon completion, these projects are expected to add a cumulative 8,000 MW to the national grid. The reply also included five-year equity sanction, release and utilization data for each project.
enrichment.context:
India's nuclear power expansion is central to its strategy for energy security and decarbonization, aiming to increase nuclear capacity substantially by 2031-32 as part of the broader push toward non-fossil fuel energy sources under India's Panchamrit and Net Zero 2070 commitments. Projects like the Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant (KKNPP) involve Russian cooperation under an inter-governmental agreement, making them susceptible to geopolitical disruptions such as the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Similarly, indigenous projects like the Indigenous Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (IPHWR) and the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam are significant milestones in India's three-stage nuclear power programme, with PFBR being a key step toward utilizing thorium reserves in the long run.

Delays in nuclear projects have historically been a matter of parliamentary and public scrutiny, given the high capital costs and strategic importance of these plants. The Fukushima disaster in 2011 led to comprehensive safety re-evaluations globally, including in India, causing design revisions. The COVID-19 pandemic further disrupted supply chains and labour availability at plant sites. This periodic disclosure of project status, costs, and equity utilization reflects the government's accountability mechanism for large public sector infrastructure investments, and is routinely used to assess progress against India's nuclear capacity addition targets.

prelims_questions.question: Which of the following nuclear power projects in India involves foreign (Russian) cooperation, as per government data on nuclear projects under construction?
prelims_questions.explanation: The Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant (KKNPP) units are Light Water Reactors built with foreign cooperation, specifically with Russia, unlike the other indigenous IPHWR projects listed.

prelims_questions.question: The Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR), mentioned in a recent Rajya Sabha reply on nuclear projects, is located at:
prelims_questions.explanation: As per the release, PFBR is located at Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu, and represents the second stage of India's three-stage nuclear power programme utilizing plutonium and thorium.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the significance of nuclear energy in India's energy security and climate commitments. Analyze the major factors causing delays in the construction of nuclear power projects in India.

mains_questions.question: Examine the three-stage nuclear power programme of India and the role of the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) in achieving long-term energy self-sufficiency through thorium utilization.
